source.title: Stable Rank Normalization for Improved Generalization in Neural Networks and GANs
source.authors: Amartya Sanyal; P. Torr; P. Dokania

record.tranche_reason: Tests the coexistence of clean-label generalization and random-label fitting using different normalization methods and generalization measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports clean-data test accuracy and random-label training accuracy, but not held-out accuracy on randomized labels. The stated chance-level test accuracy for randomized labels is background explanation, not a reported experiment result. Figure-only classification results are not assigned precise values.
record.test_reason: The study repeats label-randomization experiments and measures clean-label test accuracy, directly testing components of V1 in additional architectures and normalization settings. Random-label test accuracy is asserted from chance reasoning rather than measured.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that SRN improves classifier accuracy, reduces random-label memorization and lowers selected complexity measures, and also improves GAN training and evaluation metrics. Their complexity measures and reduced memorization are evidence they interpret as improved generalization, rather than direct measurements of every listed generalization claim.
record.recipe_differences: Uses standard SGD classification recipes but adds stable-rank and spectral normalization; tests the random-label/generalization relationship through normalization comparisons and sample-complexity measures rather than the original shattering protocol alone.
record.method_sensitivity: Normalization method and stable-rank constraint affect random-label fitting and clean-data accuracy; weight decay condition changes reported randomized-label training errors.

fits_no_version.finding: SRN often lowers Spec-Fro, Spec-L1 and Jac-Norm complexity quantities and empirical input sensitivity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stable-rank normalization can reduce selected complexity proxies and empirical Lipschitz quantities; these are not V7's magnitude-aware weight sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: SRN changes GAN Inception, FID, neural-divergence scores and discriminator sensitivity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stable-rank normalization can improve selected GAN evaluation metrics; these results do not test any listed version.

record.problems: Held-out accuracy on randomized labels is not reported. Random-label training error is used as a memorization indicator. Several classification values are presented only in plots; the text supplies limited exact clean-test numbers.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows left out; Figure 2 and Figure 3 contain per-architecture plotted outcomes that are not transcribed as precise values.

untested.parts: Measured held-out accuracy after random-label training; the original unregularized architecture configurations; and whether incomplete fitting persists with longer training. Clean and random-label experiments do not uniformly share the same learning rate or epoch budget.
Width sweeps past the interpolation threshold and their test-error trajectories.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under controlled tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Effects of dropout and its interaction with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its correlation with measured generalization gaps, and its ranking against competing measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random removal and retraining.

missing.what: Matched clean-label results for Table 1's low-learning-rate protocol: Table 7 reports approximately 69–71% test accuracy across methods and weight-decay conditions. Record these to pair clean generalization with R1–R2. The surrounding text identifies CIFAR100 and low learning rate, whereas the caption says CIFAR10 and high learning rate; preserve this source inconsistency.
missing.locator: Appendix D.1, Table 7 and preceding paragraph

missing.what: CIFAR10 clean-label and random-label experiments extend the paired comparison beyond CIFAR100. Record per-model, per-method results when readable; the supplied text only states that SRN improves clean accuracy and reduces random-label fitting.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V1. Support labels concern measured components, not a complete replication of V1's conjunction. Explicit normalization, weight decay, finite training budgets and recipe differences prevent treating reduced random-label fitting as a challenge to the original unregularized result. Figures 2 and 3 are already declared as incompletely transcribed in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out accuracy on randomized labels is not reported; the paper does not test Inception, AlexNet, or MLPs in the specific configurations named in the version.
The paper measures sample-complexity quantities and empirical Lipschitz behavior, but not magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures as defined in this version.

rows.subject: ResNet-110
rows.operation_detail: Trained with randomized CIFAR100 labels; compared weight decay and normalization conditions.
rows.note: Lower training error means more fitting of randomized labels. Results are reported for each method; the text does not give test accuracy on randomized labels.
rows.check: Values are correct, but split the four normalization methods into separate rows. Training errors of 10.56–12.02% show substantial but incomplete random-label fitting after 200 epochs; they do not establish near-perfect fitting.

rows.subject: ResNet110
rows.operation_detail: Trained on clean CIFAR100 and evaluated on the test set with different normalization methods.
rows.note: The text gives this comparison directly; the figure reports additional values without numerical transcription.
rows.check: 71.5% clean-label test accuracy is far above CIFAR100's 1% chance level. Use chance as the claim-relevant baseline. This standard-recipe experiment is not the clean counterpart of the low-learning-rate Table 1 experiment.

source_check.correct: Section 5.1 states SN test accuracy 71.5% without a numerical Vanilla comparison there. Figure 1 separately reports Vanilla 72.4%, SN 71.5% and SRN 73.1%; retain that locator distinction.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1, numerical ResNet110 example; Section 3, Figure 1 caption.
source_check.problem: Vanilla accuracy is stated elsewhere in the text, so an unqualified not-stated baseline is misleading.

rows.subject: ResNet110
rows.operation_detail: Trained on clean CIFAR100 and evaluated on the test set with different normalization methods.
rows.note: The paper reports this as an example of improved clean-data accuracy.
rows.check: 73.2% clean-label test accuracy establishes the clean-generalization component. Improvement over SN is not itself V1's effect; use the 1% chance baseline when assessing V1.

rows.subject: ResNet-110, WideResNet-28-10, AlexNet, DenseNet-100, VGG-19
rows.operation_detail: Compared clean-data test accuracy across Vanilla, SN, and SRN training.
rows.value: SRN test accuracy is higher than Vanilla and SN across the architectures, except SRN-50 and SN are almost equal for AlexNet.
rows.uncertainty: 75% confidence interval; five runs with new random seeds
rows.note: Aggregate textual comparison across the five architectures; individual plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: The recorded value ranks normalization methods rather than reporting absolute accuracy relative to chance. Split by architecture and method and record clean test accuracies when readable. Near equality between SRN and SN on AlexNet is not partial evidence for V1.

rows.subject: ResNet-110, WideResNet-28-10, AlexNet, DenseNet-100, VGG-19
rows.operation_detail: Compared training accuracy on randomized-label CIFAR100 across normalization methods.
rows.value: SRN reduces training accuracy on randomized labels; the same model achieved the highest training accuracy when labels were not randomized.
rows.note: The text summarizes the cross-architecture result; Figure 3 values are not numerically transcribed.
rows.check: A relative reduction in random-label training accuracy cannot establish whether each model fits nearly perfectly. Split by architecture and method and record absolute fitting levels. VGG's random-label learning rate was reduced to 0.01 because it failed to learn at the larger rate, so its clean and random-label recipes differ.
